title: Generate Content
summary: Generate Content covers the adversary work of producing written, audio, visual, or multimedia material that supports targeting and operations, rather than producing code. The material itself is the payload of persuasion: personas, impersonated organisations, pretexts, forged documents, and influence narratives tailored to a specific victim or region. It can be authored in house, commissioned from third parties, or produced with AI-assisted tools, and it may be researched and drafted before an operation begins. Because the artefacts are ordinary business text or media, they leave little host telemetry; the reliable evidence sits in mail and collaboration platforms, in sender and domain registration data, and in the writing itself, for example mismatched signatures, unfamiliar phrasing, or urgency used where routine process expects none. Defenders distinguish it from legitimate correspondence by comparing claimed identity against authenticated headers, by checking whether the request matches the sender's normal role and history, and by looking for content reused across many recipients.

beginner.definition: Generating content means an attacker creates written, sound, or picture material to help a trick work. It includes fake emails, fake invoices, fake job adverts, and fake profile pages. The attacker builds this material before or during an attack. It is not computer code and it does not break into anything by itself.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most attacks start by fooling a person, and people believe messages that look and sound real. Attackers need good content to make a fake request seem normal. When the content is convincing, employees approve payments, reset passwords, or open links they should refuse. This is why a polished forgery is often more dangerous than a technical exploit. Attackers can now mass produce it with AI tools.
howItWorks: The attacker studies the target organisation, and learns names, roles, projects, and writing style from public sources.
They decide the story, which is called a pretext, such as an urgent invoice or a job offer.
They write or generate the message, image, voice recording, or video that carries that story.
They may translate it, or copy the tone of a trusted sender, so it fits the target audience.
They deliver it through email, chat, phone, social media, or a fake profile.
They keep the persona alive with more messages, so the victim never doubts it.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel front desk at night. A caller says he is the manager. He asks the clerk to hand over a spare key card for room 402. The caller uses the manager's first name, mentions the correct shift times, and speaks calmly. Nothing physical was forced, and no lock was broken. The story did all the work. The clerk simply believed the story. Generated content is the script, the accent, and the paperwork the caller prepared before making that phone call.
takeaways: Generated content is the material used to persuade you, not computer code.
A message can look perfect and still be false, so check the request, not the style.
Attackers can produce this content quickly and in many languages.

objectives: Explain what content generation means and why it is not the same as writing malware.
Describe how attackers research a target before writing a pretext.
Identify the types of material that can be generated, including text, audio, and video.
Recognise which later techniques usually consume generated content, such as phishing.
Explain which artefacts help analysts spot fabricated content in email and collaboration tools.
